**Acid-Base Disorders** ★★ — Identify primary disorder (pH ==7.35-7.45==), always correct AG for albumin (==+2.5== per 1 g/dL <4.0), and check compensation + delta-delta to catch mixed disorders.

- **Flow:** pH (<7.35 acidaemia, >7.45 alkalaemia) → primary disorder → if metabolic acidosis: **AG** + **albumin correction** → **Winter's formula** → if AG >12: **delta-delta ratio**.

## Reference ranges & formulas

| Metric | Normal / Formula | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| pH / PaCO₂ / HCO₃⁻ | ==7.35-7.45== · ==35-45 mmHg== · ==22-26 mEq/L== | Acidaemia <7.35; alkalaemia >7.45 |
| Anion gap (AG) ★ | $\text{Na}^+ - (\text{Cl}^- + \text{HCO}_3^-)$ = ==8-12 mEq/L== | >12 = HAGMA (methanol, uraemia, DKA, propylene glycol, INH/iron, lactate, ethylene glycol, salicylates); normal = NAGMA (RTA, diarrhoea, 0.9% saline) |
| Corrected AG ★★ | ==$\text{AG} + 2.5 \times (4.0 - \text{Albumin})$== | Hypoalbuminaemia hides elevated AG |
| Winter's formula ★★ | ==$\text{PaCO}_2 = 1.5 \times [\text{HCO}_3^-] + 8 \pm 2\text{ mmHg}$== | Measured > upper limit = + resp acidosis; < lower limit = + resp alkalosis |
| Metabolic alkalosis | ↑PaCO₂ ==0.7 mmHg== per +1 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ >24 | Capped ==<55 mmHg== (hypoxaemia limits hypoventilation) |

## Respiratory compensation (vs)

| Primary disorder | Acute (per 10 mmHg PaCO₂) | Chronic (>3-5 days, per 10 mmHg PaCO₂) |
|---|---|---|
| **Respiratory acidosis (PaCO₂ ↑)** ★ | HCO₃⁻ ==↑ 1 mEq/L== | HCO₃⁻ ==↑ 3.5-4 mEq/L== |
| **Respiratory alkalosis (PaCO₂ ↓)** ★ | HCO₃⁻ ==↓ 2 mEq/L== | HCO₃⁻ ==↓ 4-5 mEq/L== |

## Delta-delta ratio (HAGMA)

$$\frac{\text{AG}_{\text{corrected}} - 12}{24 - [\text{HCO}_3^-]}$$

| Ratio | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ==<1== | Concurrent non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) |
| ==1 to 2== | Pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) |
| ==>2== | Concurrent metabolic alkalosis or pre-existing chronic respiratory acidosis |

## ⚠ Never

- ==Never assume normal pH excludes an acid-base disorder== — normal pH + abnormal PaCO₂ & HCO₃⁻ proves a **mixed disorder** (compensation ==never== fully normalises pH ==except possibly in mild chronic respiratory alkalosis==) ★★.
- ==Do not rapidly overcorrect chronic respiratory acidosis== with aggressive ventilation → post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis → arrhythmias & seizures ★★.

## Cards

- Normal arterial pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻, and anion gap ranges → pH 7.35-7.45, PaCO₂ 35-45 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22-26 mEq/L, AG 8-12 mEq/L
- How do you correct the anion gap for hypoalbuminaemia? → Add 2.5 mEq/L to measured AG for every 1.0 g/dL albumin below 4.0 g/dL
- Winter's formula and how to read deviations → Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × [HCO₃⁻] + 8 ± 2 mmHg; higher = concomitant respiratory acidosis, lower = concomitant respiratory alkalosis
- Acute vs chronic HCO₃⁻ change per 10 mmHg PaCO₂ in respiratory acidosis and alkalosis → Acidosis: ↑1 acute / ↑3.5-4 chronic; alkalosis: ↓2 acute / ↓4-5 chronic (mEq/L)
- Interpret delta-delta ratio <1, 1-2, and >2 in HAGMA → <1 = +NAGMA; 1-2 = pure HAGMA; >2 = +metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis
- Does a normal pH exclude an acid-base disorder? → No; compensation never fully normalises pH (except possibly mild chronic respiratory alkalosis), so normal pH with abnormal PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ proves a mixed disorder
- Why must you not rapidly overcorrect chronic respiratory acidosis? → Causes post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis, which can precipitate arrhythmias and seizures
